title: Specifying and Staging Mixed-Initiative Dialogs with Program Generation and Transformation
review_status: full-text audit complete; formal dialog-space/compression analysis, Scheme proof-of-concept dialog miner/stager, implementation details, venue metadata limits, and targeted 2025 follow-up checked
sections_checked: Abstract/introduction and dialog model
Section 3.2: combinatorial/formal expressiveness analysis, not a user experiment
Sections 5.1–5.6: Scheme proof of concept, dialog mining and generated stagers
Section 6: contribution claims and limitations
venue_year_verified: arXiv v5 PDF dated 2015-12-21; original conference/journal venue not independently verified in this audit; the selected frame period is arXiv first submission 2011
evidence_note: The paper argues partial evaluation can stage mixed-initiative dialogs and supplies a Scheme proof-of-concept toolkit. Its ‘Evaluation’ section counts/formally classifies dialog specifications; it does not measure task success, user errors, or independent authoring effort. A later 2025 journal extension adds a Haskell implementation and food-ordering case study with compression comparisons, but not controlled end-user outcome evidence.

title: Typing Context-Dependent Behavioural Variation
review_status: full-text audit complete; operational semantics, explicit-context assumptions, progress and subject-reduction lemmas, future-work boundary, and targeted security extension checked
sections_checked: Abstract and Section 2: ContextML context stack and dispatch semantics
Type-system soundness: Lemmas 2.1 (progress) and 2.2 (subject reduction)
Section 3: explicit-context scope and asynchronous/event-driven evolution as future work
evidence_note: ContextML's type system guarantees that well-typed dispatch does not get stuck under its formal explicit-context semantics. The authors distinguish this from asynchronous environment evolution and event-driven context changes, which they leave for future work. The related COORDINATION 2012 security paper adds message-driven context changes and static policy/protocol checks, but still proposes concurrency, distribution, and asynchrony extensions as future work.

title: The Complexity of Flow Analysis in Higher-Order Languages
review_status: full-text audit complete; dissertation provenance/date, preface scope, 0CFA/kCFA/exact-kCFA complexity results, conclusion and future-work claims, and targeted PLDI 2010 counter-scope evidence checked
sections_checked: Title page and dissertation acceptance: Brandeis PhD dissertation, August 2009
Abstract and Preface: theorem-only scope; explicitly no benchmarks or prototype implementations
Chapters 3 and 5: 0CFA PTIME-complete and kCFA EXPTIME-complete for fixed k>0 in the specified functional formulation
Section 5.6: exact kCFA PTIME-complete
Chapter 7: open directions for polynomial polyvariant flow analyses
venue_year_verified: Brandeis University PhD dissertation, August 2009; first arXiv submission 2013-11-19, so the frozen arXiv-date stratum is not the work's origin year
evidence_note: The dissertation gives formal worst-case complexity results for specified higher-order functional-language analyses and explicitly disclaims benchmark/prototype evaluation. A PLDI 2010 follow-up shows a polynomial-time OO formulation, derives polynomial m-CFA for functional programs, and reports empirical precision/cost results, so the theorem must not be generalized across languages or taken as a practical-runtime curve.

review_status: targeted primary-source full-text follow-up; official journal metadata and full-text abstract/results checked for semantics, Haskell implementation, case study, compression outcome, and stated evaluation scope

Formal semantics and Haskell proof-of-concept implementation claims
Online-food-ordering case study, compression result, and comparisons to VoiceXML/SCXML
venue_year_verified: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming, 2025, Vol. 10, Issue 1, Article 7; DOI 10.22152/programming-journal.org/2025/10/7
evidence_note: This is direct later work on the sampled 2011 dialog DSL: it adds coroutine-like concurrent subdialogs, formalizes staging, provides a Haskell implementation, and reports a food-ordering case study/compression benefit. It is substantive counterevidence to saying the line never progressed beyond a prototype, but the official description does not report controlled user completion/time/error outcomes.

title: Types for Coordinating Secure Behavioural Variations
review_status: targeted primary-source full-text follow-up; ContextML extension, message-driven context evolution, static resource/protocol verification, abstract communication model, and future-work boundary checked
sections_checked: Abstract and Sections 1–3: ContextML extension, resources, security, and message passing
Sections 4–6: effects and policy/protocol model checking
Section 7: conclusion and explicit concurrency/distribution/asynchrony future work
evidence_note: This same-group extension adds context changes triggered by the program and exchanged messages, resource/security policies, and static effects/model checking. Its communication bus remains abstract, and the conclusion explicitly leaves a richer coordination model with concurrency, distribution, and asynchrony for future work. It narrows but does not remove the deployment/runtime boundary identified in the 2013 ContextML paper.

title: Resolving and Exploiting the k-CFA Paradox
review_status: targeted primary-source full-text follow-up; inspected language/representation distinction, polynomial m-CFA construction, empirical precision/cost comparisons, and scope claims
sections_checked: Introduction: functional EXPTIME theorem versus OO polynomial formulations
Sections 2–5: closure/object representations and polynomial m-CFA construction
Section 6 and conclusion: empirical precision/runtime comparisons and caveats
venue_year_verified: ACM SIGPLAN PLDI 2010; arXiv v1 posted 2013-11-17 (the frame's arXiv period is distinct from venue year)
evidence_note: The paper explains that the complexity split arises from interaction between call-context sensitivity and closure versus object representation; it derives polynomial m-CFA for functional programs and reports m-CFA as comparably precise at lower cost on its evaluated cases. This is direct counter-scope to treating the dissertation's functional worst-case result as a general statement about OO analyses or all practical programs.
